A [reflection](mathematics/reflection) is a [transformation](mathematics/transformation) that produces a 
mirror image of an [object](mathematics/object) across a line, point, or plane (the axis of 
reflection), so that each point and its image are the same distance from the axis but on opposite sides.

---

Reflecting the point (2, 3) across the y-axis produces the point (-2, 3): the x-coordinate is negated while 
the y-coordinate stays the same, placing the image the same distance from the axis but on the opposite side.

nodes.title: rotation
nodes.content:
# rotation


A [rotation](mathematics/rotation) is a [transformation](mathematics/transformation) that turns an 
[object](mathematics/object) around a fixed point (the center of rotation) by a given angle, 
keeping the distance from each point to the center unchanged.

---

Rotating the point (1, 0) by 90 degrees counterclockwise around the origin produces the point (0, 1): the 
point's distance from the origin (1) stays the same, but its position turns around the center by the given 
angle.

nodes.title: symmetry
nodes.content:
# symmetry


Symmetry is a [relation](mathematics/relation) between an 
[object](mathematics/object) and an [operation](mathematics/operation) where applying 
the operation leaves the object unchanged in the aspects being considered. A symmetric object therefore has a 
form or behavior that is preserved under some [transformation](mathematics/transformation), such as 
[reflection](mathematics/reflection), [rotation](mathematics/rotation), or exchange 
of parts.

---

A [palindrome](mathematics/palindrome) exhibits symmetry under the operation of reversal:
reversing the sequence (1, 2, 3, 2, 1) leaves it unchanged. In contrast, reversing the sequence (1, 2, 3)
yields (3, 2, 1), which is different from the original, so this sequence does not exhibit symmetry under
reversal.

nodes.title: data
nodes.content:
# data


A collection of discrete or continuous values that convey [information](mathematics/information), 
describing quantities, qualities, facts, or simply sequences of symbols that may be further interpreted 
formally.

---

The [numbers](mathematics/number) (72, 85, 90) are data representing three exam scores. On their own they are just values, but when
interpreted as "scores out of 100", they convey information about how well a group of students performed.

nodes.title: dataset
nodes.content:
# dataset


A [dataset](computer_science/dataset) is a [set](mathematics/set) of [data](computer_science/data), 
typically organized as records or examples for analysis, training, or testing.

---

A table of 100 rows, each containing a student's exam scores across five subjects, is a dataset: it is a set
of data records that can be analyzed to study student performance.

nodes.title: data_structure
nodes.content:
# data_structure


A [data_structure](computer_science/data_structure) is a way of organizing and storing [data](computer_science/data) so it can be 
accessed and modified [efficiently](mathematics/efficiency). A data structure contains a value or group 
of values and the [functions](mathematics/function) or 
[operations](mathematics/operation) that can be applied to the data.

---

A list of exam scores (72, 85, 90), together with operations such as "add a score" or "find the highest score",
forms a data structure: the values are organized in a sequence and paired with the functions that act on them.

nodes.title: object
nodes.content:
# object


An [object](computer_science/object) is an instance of a [data structure](computer_science/data_structure).

---

The array (72, 85, 90) is an object: it is one specific instance of the array data structure, holding these
particular [numbers](mathematics/number).

nodes.title: operation
nodes.content:
# operation


[operation](computer_science/operation) is an action that is carried out to accomplish a given task. In the most simple scenario, 
it is an action performed on at least one [object](computer_science/object).

---

Appending a new score to the object (72, 85, 90), producing (72, 85, 90, 91), is an operation: it is an action
carried out on that object to accomplish the task of adding a value.

nodes.title: bit
nodes.content:
# bit


The [bit](computer_science/bit) (binary digit) is the smallest unit of data in computing, representing a binary state of 
either 0 or 1. Bits are the fundamental building blocks of [data](computer_science/data) and can convey basic 
forms of [information](mathematics/information) by representing true/false or on/off states.

---

The sequence 1011 consists of four bits — 1, 0, 1, and 1 — each representing a binary state that can convey
one basic unit of information, such as on or off.

nodes.title: data_type
nodes.content:
# data_type


Data type (or simply type) is a grouping of [data](computer_science/data) values, usually specified by a 
[set](mathematics/set) of possible values, a [set](mathematics/set) of allowed 
[operations](mathematics/operation) on these values, and/or a representation of these values as 
machine types.

---

For example, the 8-bit unsigned integer data type is defined by its set of possible values (0 through 255), a
set of allowed operations such as addition and comparison, and a representation as a sequence of 8
[bits](computer_science/bit) in memory.

nodes.title: binary_representation
nodes.content:
# binary representation


[binary_representation](computer_science/binary_representation) is a way of expressing [information](mathematics/information) using only two symbols, 
typically 0 and 1. In this system, each digit is called a [bit](computer_science/bit), and 
[sequences](mathematics/sequence) of bits are used to represent [numbers](mathematics/number) 
and other types of information.

---

The number 13 has the binary representation 1101: reading the bits from left to right as powers of two gives
1x2^3 + 1x2^2 + 0x2^1 + 1x2^0 = 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13.

nodes.title: hexadecimal_code
nodes.content:
# hexadecimal code


[hexadecimal_code](computer_science/hexadecimal_code) is a representation of a [value](mathematics/number) written in the 
hexadecimal [numeral system](mathematics/numeral_system).

Hexadecimal is a positional numeral system with [radix](mathematics/radix) 16, 
commonly using digits 0-9 and letters A-F.

---

The decimal number 255 is represented in hexadecimal as FF: reading right to left, F is 15 in the ones place
and F is 15 in the sixteens place, so 15x16 + 15 = 240 + 15 = 255.

nodes.title: binary_fractions
nodes.content:
# binary fractions


[binary_fractions](computer_science/binary_fractions) are a way to represent fractional [numbers](mathematics/number) 
using [binary representation](computer_science/binary_representation). In binary fractions, 
[bits](computer_science/bit) to the right of a binary point represent negative powers of 2 
(1/2, 1/4, 1/8, etc.), similar to how digits after a decimal point in base-10 represent 
negative powers of 10.

---

The binary fraction 0.101 represents 1/2 + 0/4 + 1/8 = 5/8.

nodes.title: bitwise_operation
nodes.content:
# bitwise operation


[bitwise_operation](computer_science/bitwise_operation) is an [operation](computer_science/operation) that acts on individual [bits](computer_science/bit) 
within a [binary_representation](computer_science/binary_representation). Bitwise operations work directly on the bits of 
[data](computer_science/data), allowing for [efficient](mathematics/efficiency) manipulation and comparison 
at the lowest level of representation.

---

Applying the bitwise [AND](mathematics/and) operation to 1010 and 1100 produces 1000:
each output bit is 1 only where both corresponding input bits are 1.

nodes.title: bitmask
nodes.content:
# bitmask


A [bitmask](computer_science/bitmask) is a [binary representation](computer_science/binary_representation) pattern 
whose [bits](computer_science/bit) are used with 
[bitwise operations](computer_science/bitwise_operation) to select, set, clear, toggle, or test corresponding 
bits in another [value](mathematics/number).

---

The bitmask 0010 can be combined with a bitwise [AND operation](mathematics/and) on 0110 to 
test whether bit 1 is set: 0010 AND 0110 = 0010, which is nonzero, so bit 1 of 0110 is set.

nodes.title: hamming_weight
nodes.content:
# Hamming weight


The [hamming_weight](computer_science/hamming_weight) of a [binary representation](computer_science/binary_representation) is the 
[number](mathematics/number) of [bits](computer_science/bit) whose value is 1. It is also 
called the population count or the number of set bits.

---

The binary representation 1011 has a Hamming weight of 3, since three of its four bits (the two rightmost
bits and the leftmost bit) are set to 1.

nodes.title: bottleneck
nodes.content:
# bottleneck


A [bottleneck](computer_science/bottleneck) is a part of a system that limits overall
[performance](mathematics/real_world_performance) because it is the slowest or most
[constrained](mathematics/constraint) step.

In [algorithm](mathematics/algorithm) analysis, a bottleneck is often the
[operation](computer_science/operation) that dominates the
[complexity](mathematics/complexity).

---

An algorithm first sorts a list of n elements in [O(n log n)](mathematics/big_o_notation) time, then 
scans it once in [O(n)](mathematics/big_o_notation) time. The sorting step is the bottleneck, since its 
complexity grows faster than the scanning step as n increases, so it dominates the algorithm's overall running time.

nodes.title: computer
nodes.content:
# computer


[computer](computer_science/computer) is a device that can execute [instructions](mathematics/instruction)
to process [information](mathematics/information) and perform tasks automatically. A computer can store, retrieve, and
manipulate [data](computer_science/data) according to instructions.

---

A pocket calculator is a simple computer: it takes [numbers](mathematics/number) such as 7 and 5 as
[input_data](mathematics/input_data), follows the built-in instruction "multiply", and outputs the data 35.

nodes.title: program
nodes.content:
# program


[program](computer_science/program) is a [sequence](mathematics/sequence) of [instructions](mathematics/instruction) that 
a [computer](computer_science/computer) can execute to perform a specific task. A program defines the 
[operations](computer_science/operation) that should be carried out and the order in which they should be executed.

---

A program that computes the average of exam scores implements an [algorithm](mathematics/algorithm) as a concrete sequence 
of instructions: read each score, add them, then divide by the count. The same algorithm can be expressed by many
different programs.

nodes.title: bug
nodes.content:
# bug


A [bug](computer_science/bug) is an error or defect in a system, [program](computer_science/program), or
[algorithm](mathematics/algorithm) that causes it to behave incorrectly or produce unexpected results.

---

A program meant to compute the average of exam scores contains the [instruction](mathematics/instruction)
"divide by the count minus one" instead of "divide by the count". This bug makes every reported average too large,
so the program silently produces incorrect results rather than failing visibly.

nodes.title: hardware
nodes.content:
# hardware


[hardware](computer_science/hardware) refers to the physical, tangible components of a [computer](computer_science/computer) —
the parts that can be touched. Hardware is contrasted with
[programs](computer_science/program) (software), which are the intangible
[instructions](mathematics/instruction) the hardware executes to process 
[data](computer_science/data).

---

A keyboard is hardware: a physical device with keys that lets a user type [information](mathematics/information)
into the computer.

nodes.title: computer_memory
nodes.content:
# computer memory


[computer_memory](computer_science/computer_memory) is a [hardware](computer_science/hardware) component that stores [data](computer_science/data) 
for immediate use by a [computer](computer_science/computer). It provides storage for 
[instructions](mathematics/instruction) and data that are actively being processed or accessed, enabling the 
computer to perform [operations](computer_science/operation) efficiently.

---

When you open a photo, the [information](mathematics/information) describing its pixels is loaded from disk into memory so 
that each edit appears instantly while you work. If power is lost before saving, the in-memory contents disappear —
illustrating that this storage is volatile, unlike the disk it was loaded from.

nodes.title: disk
nodes.content:
# disk


[disk](computer_science/disk) is a [hardware](computer_science/hardware) component that stores
[data](computer_science/data) persistently, retaining it even when power is turned off (non-volatile
storage). A disk provides long-term retention of large amounts of data that programs can read or write.

---

A hard disk drive (HDD) or solid-state drive (SSD) in a laptop is a disk: documents, photos, and installed
programs remain stored on it after the computer is shut down and are available again when it next starts.

nodes.title: file_storage
nodes.content:
# file storage


[file_storage](computer_science/file_storage) is the persistent retention of [data](computer_science/data) organized as
named files, typically held on a [disk](computer_science/disk). Storing data as named files lets
programs locate, read, and update it by name rather than by physical location on the disk.

---

On a laptop, saving a text document places its data into a named file on the disk. Reopening the document later
reads that file back from the disk, and the content survives shutdown because disk storage is persistent.

nodes.title: input_output
nodes.content:
# input output


[input_output](computer_science/input_output) (I/O) is the transfer of [data](computer_science/data) between a computer and
the outside world. Input is data received into the system, while output is data sent out; both flow through
[hardware](computer_science/hardware) devices.

---

A keyboard provides input: each key press sends data into the computer. A display provides output: the computer
sends data out to be shown on the screen. Together these devices let a person interact with a running program.

nodes.title: processor
nodes.content:
# processor


[processor](computer_science/processor) is a [hardware](computer_science/hardware) component of a [computer](computer_science/computer) 
that executes [instructions](mathematics/instruction) and performs [operations](computer_science/operation) 
on [data](computer_science/data). It is the central component responsible for carrying out the computational 
tasks defined by [programs](computer_science/program), often referred to as the central processing unit (CPU).

---

When a program instructs the processor to add two numbers, the processor fetches the instruction, reads the two
input values from [memory](computer_science/computer_memory), executes the addition, and writes the result 
back — repeating this cycle millions of times per second to run an entire program containing thousands of instructions.

nodes.title: concurrency
nodes.content:
# concurrency


[concurrency](computer_science/concurrency) is the ability of a [program](computer_science/program) to execute multiple tasks or 
[operations](computer_science/operation) simultaneously or in overlapping time periods. In concurrent execution, 
multiple streams of [instructions](mathematics/instruction) make progress without necessarily running at the 
exact same instant, allowing for more efficient use of system resources and improved responsiveness. Concurrency 
enables programs to handle multiple operations such as user input or background processing at the same time.

---

A web browser that downloads images while the user scrolls a page is not running both tasks at the
exact same instant on a single [processor](computer_science/processor). Instead, the processor rapidly switches between the two 
instruction streams, so each makes progress and the application stays responsive.

nodes.title: parallelism
nodes.content:
# parallelism


[parallelism](computer_science/parallelism) is a form of [concurrency](computer_science/concurrency) where multiple 
[operations](computer_science/operation) or tasks are executed simultaneously at the exact same time, typically by 
utilizing multiple [processors](computer_science/processor) or processing units. Unlike 
[concurrency](computer_science/concurrency), which is about managing multiple tasks that may overlap in time, 
[parallelism](computer_science/parallelism) specifically requires the physical simultaneous execution of tasks. This approach enables 
[programs](computer_science/program) to achieve significant performance improvements by dividing work across 
multiple processing units.

---

Rendering a 4K video frame can be split into four [quadrants](mathematics/quadrant), each assigned to a 
separate processor that applies the same stream of [instructions](mathematics/instruction) to its quadrant at 
the exact same instant. All four finish together, so the frame renders roughly four times faster than on a single 
processor — true parallel execution, not just overlapping progress.

nodes.title: core
nodes.content:
# core


[core](computer_science/core) is an independent processing unit within a [processor](computer_science/processor) 
that can execute [instructions](mathematics/instruction) and perform [operations](computer_science/operation) 
independently of other cores. Modern processors often contain multiple cores, enabling them to execute multiple 
tasks simultaneously, which is essential for [parallel computing](computer_science/parallelism).

---

A quad-core processor has four cores, each running its own stream of instructions. While one core renders video
frames for a [program](computer_science/program), the other three can handle audio decoding, network input, and user
interface updates — all at the same time, with each core unaware of the others' work.

nodes.title: programming_language
nodes.content:
# programming language


A [programming_language](computer_science/programming_language) is a formal system of syntax and vocabulary used to write 
[programs](computer_science/program) as text. It defines which sequences of 
[instructions](mathematics/instruction) are valid and what each one means, so that a 
[computer](computer_science/computer) can parse and execute them.

---

Different programming languages use different symbols and keywords for the same operation. The instruction "add
two numbers" might be written with a `+` symbol in one language, a keyword like `ADD` in another, or a single
symbol in a third. Each language provides its own syntax for expressing the same underlying instruction.

nodes.title: code
nodes.content:
# code


[code](computer_science/code) is the textual form of a [program](computer_science/program) written in a
[programming language](computer_science/programming_language). It is a sequence of
[instructions](mathematics/instruction) expressed using the syntax and vocabulary of a specific language
so that a [computer](computer_science/computer) can parse and execute it.

---

The same instruction "add two numbers" can be written as code in many different programming languages. In one
language it might appear as `a + b`, in another as a keyword like `ADD`, and in yet another as a single symbol.
Each snippet is valid code in its own language, but the underlying instruction is the same — only the textual
representation differs.

nodes.title: over_optimization
nodes.content:
# over-optimization


[over_optimization](computer_science/over_optimization) is the act of applying [optimization](mathematics/optimization) 
beyond what is justified by the requirements.

Over-optimization can make a [program](computer_science/program) harder to understand and maintain, 
and may not yield meaningful [performance](mathematics/real_world_performance) benefits.

---

A program that processes 100 records per day is over-optimized if a developer rewrites its simple loop into
obfuscated bitwise tricks purely to improve the [time_complexity](mathematics/time_complexity) from 
[O(n)](mathematics/big_o_notation) to [O(n/2)](mathematics/big_o_notation). The
theoretical gain is negligible at this scale, but the tricks make the code far harder to read, debug, and extend.

nodes.title: pseudocode
nodes.content:
# pseudocode


[pseudocode](computer_science/pseudocode) is an informal, human-readable description of the steps of an 
[algorithm](mathematics/algorithm) or [program](computer_science/program), 
written in a way that resembles [code](computer_science/code) but is not tied to any specific language.
Pseudocode is used to communicate ideas and logic without implementation details.

---

To describe finding the largest value in a list, pseudocode might read: "set max to the first element; for each
remaining element, if it is greater than max, update max; return max." Each line is an
[instruction](mathematics/instruction) a programmer could later translate into any language —
Python, Java, or C — without changing the underlying logic.

nodes.title: if_statement
nodes.content:
# if-statement


An [if_statement](computer_science/if_statement) is a [control_structure](mathematics/control_structure) that executes a block of
[instructions](mathematics/instruction) only when a given 
[condition](mathematics/boolean_expression) evaluates to true. It is the most direct way to make 
execution depend on the [program](computer_science/program)'s state or input.

---

"If the temperature is above 30, turn on the fan" is an if-statement: the condition "temperature above 30" is
checked, and the instruction "turn on the fan" runs only when that condition holds. When the condition is false,
the instruction is skipped and execution continues with whatever follows.

nodes.title: branch
nodes.content:
# branch


A [branch](computer_science/branch) is one possible [path](mathematics/path) of execution in a
[program](computer_science/program), typically chosen by evaluating a 
[condition](mathematics/boolean_expression).

---

An [if_statement](computer_science/if_statement) creates two branches: one taken when the condition is true, the other when it is false. Each
branch holds its own sequence of [instructions](mathematics/instruction), and exactly one of the two
sequences runs on any given execution — the choice between them is what makes the program's behavior depend on
its input.

nodes.title: right_shift
nodes.content:
# right shift


[right_shift](computer_science/right_shift) is a [bitwise operation](computer_science/bitwise_operation) 
that shifts all [bits](computer_science/bit) in a 
[binary representation](computer_science/binary_representation) to the right by a 
specified number of positions. Right shift by one position is equivalent to 
[integer](mathematics/integer) division by 2.

---

Shifting the 8-bit value 11001100 (204) right by two positions yields 00110011 (51), which is exactly 204 // 4.
The two rightmost bits are discarded; what fills the vacated positions on the left depends on which variant of
right shift is used.

nodes.title: reverse_engineering
nodes.content:
# reverse engineering


[reverse_engineering](computer_science/reverse_engineering) is the process of analyzing a [program](computer_science/program) or system to 
discover its components, structure, and [operation](computer_science/operation), often by examining its 
[data](computer_science/data) and behavior, without access to its source [code](computer_science/code). 
Reverse engineering is used to understand how something works.

---

Given a program whose source code is unavailable, an engineer studies what it does for many different inputs:
"input 5 gives 25, input 6 gives 36, input 7 gives 49." From these observations the engineer infers that the
underlying [algorithm](mathematics/algorithm) squares the input — reconstructing the logic from behavior alone,
without ever reading the original code.

nodes.title: logical_right_shift
nodes.content:
# logical right shift


[logical_right_shift](computer_science/logical_right_shift) is a [bitwise operation](computer_science/bitwise_operation) 
and a variant of [right shift](computer_science/right_shift) that always fills the 
leftmost [bits](computer_science/bit) with zeros, regardless of the sign of the 
[integer](mathematics/integer). This [operation](computer_science/operation) treats the 
[binary representation](computer_science/binary_representation) as an unsigned value, 
making it suitable for unsigned integer division by powers of 2.

---

The 8-bit value 10000000 (128 as unsigned) shifted right by two with logical shift gives 00100000 (32): two
zeros enter from the left, and the original sign bit is treated as ordinary data.

nodes.title: cache
nodes.content:
# cache


[cache](computer_science/cache) is a high-speed [computer_memory](computer_science/computer_memory) storage layer that temporarily 
holds frequently accessed or recently used [data](computer_science/data) to reduce access time and improve 
[performance](mathematics/real_world_performance). 
When data is requested, the cache is checked first; if the data is found (a cache hit), it can be retrieved quickly 
without accessing slower storage. If not found (a cache miss), the data must be fetched from the original source 
and may be stored in the cache for future use.

---

A common table of square roots can be kept in a cache so that a [information](mathematics/information) request for the
root of 2 is a hit on every call after the first. The first lookup computes the value and stores it (a miss); each
later lookup returns the cached value immediately instead of recomputing it.

nodes.title: test
nodes.content:
# test


A [test](computer_science/test) is a procedure or experiment used to evaluate whether a system or component
behaves as expected under specified [conditions](mathematics/criterion).

A test typically takes some [data](computer_science/data) (the [input_data](mathematics/input_data)) and produces
observations (outputs) that can be compared to expected results.

---

To test a [function](mathematics/function) that performs [sorting](mathematics/sorting) on 
[numbers](mathematics/number), one might give it the input [3, 1, 2] and check whether it returns 
[1, 2, 3]. The test passes when the actual output matches the expected output, and fails when it does not — revealing 
either a mistake in the function or a mistake in the expected result.

nodes.title: assert
nodes.content:
# assert


An [assert](computer_science/assert) is a statement in [code](computer_science/code) that checks whether a 
[condition](mathematics/criterion) holds.

Assertions are commonly used in [tests](computer_science/test) to detect unexpected states.

---

In code that computes an average, an assertion might state "the count is greater than zero" before the division
happens. If the count is in fact zero, the assertion fails immediately and stops the [program](computer_science/program) 
at that line - making the false assumption visible instead of letting a silent division-by-zero error occur later.

nodes.title: test_case
nodes.content:
# test case


A [test_case](computer_science/test_case) is a single instance of a [test](computer_science/test), defined by a specific
set of [inputs](mathematics/input_data), evaluation [criteria](mathematics/criterion), 
and expected results.

---

One test case for a [function](mathematics/function) that performs [sorting](mathematics/sorting) is: input
[3, 1, 2], expected output [1, 2, 3]. Another test case for the same function is: input [5, 5, 5] (a list where
every [number](mathematics/number) is the same), expected output [5, 5, 5]. Each test case checks the function
against one specific situation; together, many test cases build confidence that the function works in general.

nodes.title: variable
nodes.content:
# variable


[variable](computer_science/variable) is a named storage location identified by a [label](mathematics/label) 
that holds [data](computer_science/data) which can be modified during [program](computer_science/program) execution. 
A variable associates a name with a value that can change over time.

---

For example, a variable named `count` might initially hold the [number](mathematics/number) 0. Each time a relevant 
event occurs, the stored value is updated — to 1, then 2, and so on. The name `count` stays the same throughout, but 
the data at that location changes over time.

nodes.title: pointer
nodes.content:
# pointer


A [pointer](computer_science/pointer) is a [variable](computer_science/variable) whose value is a memory address: it refers to a
location in [computer_memory](computer_science/computer_memory). A pointer can be used to indirectly access
[information](mathematics/information) stored at that location.

---

Suppose memory holds a temperature reading at address 100. A pointer whose value is 100 lets a program read or
update that reading without copying it. Many pointers can refer to the same location, so an update made through
one pointer is immediately visible through any other pointer to that location.

nodes.title: memory_allocation
nodes.content:
# memory allocation


[memory_allocation](computer_science/memory_allocation) is the [operation](computer_science/operation) of assigning a block of 
[computer_memory](computer_science/computer_memory) to store [data](computer_science/data) for use by a [program](computer_science/program). 
It determines where and how much memory is reserved for storing [information](mathematics/information) during program 
execution.

---

For example, when a [program](computer_science/program) needs to store a [number](mathematics/number) for later 
use, a region of [memory](computer_science/computer_memory) is reserved, sized to hold that value, and associated 
with a [variable](computer_science/variable). Once the stored data is no longer needed, the reserved region can be released so 
the memory is available for later use.

nodes.title: deallocation
nodes.content:
# deallocation


[deallocation](computer_science/deallocation) is the [operation](computer_science/operation) of releasing a block of 
[computer_memory](computer_science/computer_memory) that was previously reserved through 
[memory_allocation](computer_science/memory_allocation), returning it to the pool of memory available for future use by a 
[program](computer_science/program).

---

For example, after a program allocates a block to hold a temporary [buffer](computer_science/data) and finishes using 
it, it deallocates the block so the same memory can be reused for a later allocation. Forgetting to deallocate blocks 
that are no longer needed gradually exhausts the available memory.

nodes.title: heap_memory
nodes.content:
# heap memory


[heap_memory](computer_science/heap_memory) is a region of [computer_memory](computer_science/computer_memory) used for dynamic 
[memory_allocation](computer_science/memory_allocation) during [program](computer_science/program) execution. It allows 
[data](computer_science/data) to be allocated and [deallocated](computer_science/deallocation) at runtime as 
needed. The heap is flexible: memory blocks can be allocated in any order and freed in any order.

---

For example, when a program creates data whose size or lifetime is not known in advance, that data is placed on the
heap. The program receives a [pointer](computer_science/pointer) to the allocated block and can access it for as long as
needed, freeing the block only when the data is no longer required.

nodes.title: heap_overflow
nodes.content:
# heap overflow


[heap_overflow](computer_science/heap_overflow) occurs when a [program](computer_science/program) attempts to use more 
[heap_memory](computer_science/heap_memory) than is available. This typically happens when too much dynamic 
[memory_allocation](computer_science/memory_allocation) occurs without proper [deallocation](computer_science/deallocation), or when attempting to 
allocate a very large amount of [computer_memory](computer_science/computer_memory) at once. When heap overflow occurs, the program 
may fail to allocate memory and typically terminates with an error.

---

For example, a program that allocates memory inside a [loop](mathematics/loop) without ever freeing it gradually fills
the heap. After enough [iterations](mathematics/iteration), the next allocation cannot find a free block large 
enough, so it fails; the program must then either handle the failure or terminate.

nodes.title: stack_memory
nodes.content:
# stack memory


[stack_memory](computer_science/stack_memory) is a region of [computer_memory](computer_science/computer_memory) used for static 
[memory_allocation](computer_science/memory_allocation) during [program](computer_science/program) execution. It stores 
[data](computer_science/data) in a [last_in_first_out](mathematics/last_in_first_out) order, automatically allocating and 
[deallocating](computer_science/deallocation) memory as [functions](mathematics/function) are called 
and return. The stack manages local [variables](computer_science/variable) and function call information.

---

For example, when a function A calls function B, which in turn calls function C, the stack grows as each function is 
entered — C on top of B on top of A — and shrinks in the reverse order as each function returns: C first, then B, then 
A. The local data of each function is removed as soon as that function returns, which is what makes the ordering 
last-in-first-out.

nodes.title: call_stack
nodes.content:
# call stack


[call_stack](computer_science/call_stack) is a region of [stack_memory](computer_science/stack_memory) that tracks active 
[function](mathematics/function) calls during [program](computer_science/program) execution. 
It stores [information](mathematics/information) about each function call, including where to return after 
the function completes. When a function is called, its information is added to the call stack, 
and when it returns, that information is removed in [last_in_first_out](mathematics/last_in_first_out) order.

---

For example, when `main` calls `compute`, which calls `save`, the call stack grows bottom-up as `main`, then `compute`, 
then `save`. When `save` returns, its entry is the first removed; `compute` then becomes the top again and resumes. The 
most recently called function is always the first to return, which is exactly the last-in-first-out rule.

nodes.title: stack_overflow
nodes.content:
# stack overflow


[stack_overflow](computer_science/stack_overflow) occurs when a [program](computer_science/program) attempts to use more 
[stack_memory](computer_science/stack_memory) than is available. This typically happens when the [call_stack](computer_science/call_stack) 
grows too large, often due to excessive [function](mathematics/function) [recursion](mathematics/recursion) or allocating 
too many local [variables](computer_science/variable). When stack overflow occurs, the program usually 
terminates with an error.

---

For example, a recursive function that calls itself on every step without ever reaching 
a [base_case](mathematics/base_case) keeps adding entries to the call stack: one for the first call, another for the 
recursive call, another for the next, and so on. Because each entry consumes stack memory, the stack eventually fills 
up and the next call cannot be placed, which is when the stack overflow occurs.

nodes.title: memory_management
nodes.content:
# memory management


[memory_management](computer_science/memory_management) is the [operation](computer_science/operation) of controlling how a [program](computer_science/program) 
uses [computer_memory](computer_science/computer_memory).

It includes when and how [memory is allocated](computer_science/memory_allocation) and 
[freed](computer_science/deallocation), and aims to use memory efficiently and safely.

---

For example, a program typically relies on two regions with different rules: the 
[stack_memory](computer_science/stack_memory) is managed automatically (memory is claimed when a function is called and released 
when it returns), while the [heap_memory](computer_science/heap_memory) is managed explicitly by the program, which must request 
blocks and later release them. Good memory management keeps each region balanced so the program neither runs out of 
memory nor holds on to memory it no longer needs.

nodes.title: twos_complement
nodes.content:
# two's complement


[twos_complement](computer_science/twos_complement) is a [binary representation](computer_science/binary_representation) method used to 
represent signed [integers](mathematics/integer) in computing. Positive [numbers](mathematics/number) 
are written in standard binary form, while a negative number is represented by inverting all 
[bits](computer_science/bit) of its positive counterpart and adding 1. This lets the same hardware circuitry perform 
arithmetic on both positive and negative values, which is why it is the most common way to represent signed integers.

---

In a 4-bit system, +5 is written as `0101`. To represent -5, invert every bit of `0101` to get `1010`, then add 1 to 
obtain `1011`. Reading `1011` as two's complement gives back -5, while the leftmost bit being 1 signals that the value 
is negative. The same addition circuit works for both signs: adding `0101` (+5) and `1011` (-5) yields `0000` with a 
discarded carry, confirming the result is 0.

nodes.title: arithmetic_right_shift
nodes.content:
# arithmetic right shift


[arithmetic_right_shift](computer_science/arithmetic_right_shift) is a [bitwise operation](computer_science/bitwise_operation) 
and a variant of [right shift](computer_science/right_shift) that preserves the sign 
[bit](computer_science/bit) when shifting signed [integers](mathematics/integer). 
Instead of filling the leftmost positions with zeros, it replicates the sign bit, 
maintaining the correct sign for negative numbers in [twos_complement](computer_science/twos_complement) 
representation. This [operation](computer_science/operation) effectively performs signed integer 
division by powers of 2.

---

The 8-bit value 10110100 (-76 in two's complement) shifted right by two with arithmetic shift 
gives 11101101 (-19): two copies of the sign bit (1) enter from the left, preserving the negative sign, and the 
result is exactly -76 // 4. A logical shift on the same bits would instead produce 00101101 (45), losing the sign.

nodes.title: deep_copy
nodes.content:
# deep copy


[deep_copy](computer_science/deep_copy) is an [operation](computer_science/operation) that creates a new 
[object](computer_science/object) with the same value as an existing object, including independent copies 
of the nested [data structures](computer_science/data_structure) it refers to. The copy uses separate 
[memory allocations](computer_science/memory_allocation), so changing nested data through one object does 
not change the other object through shared [pointers](computer_science/pointer).

---

Suppose object A holds a list that itself references two other objects, B and C. A deep copy of A produces a new object 
A' that references brand-new copies B' and C' rather than the originals. Modifying a value inside B through A leaves B' 
untouched, because A' reaches B' through its own pointers and shares no memory with A. A shallow copy of A, in contrast, 
would reuse the same B and C, so edits made through either copy would be visible through the other.

nodes.title: abstract_data_type
nodes.content:
# abstract_data_type


[abstract_data_type](computer_science/abstract_data_type) is a mathematical model of a [data type](computer_science/data_type), defined by 
its behavior from the point of view of a user of the [data](computer_science/data), specifically in terms 
of possible values, possible [operations](computer_science/operation) on data of this type, and the 
behavior of these operations.

---

For example, an abstract data type might describe a container that supports adding 
[items](mathematics/item), removing the most recently added one, and checking whether it is empty - 
a [last_in_first_out](mathematics/last_in_first_out) discipline - without specifying whether the items are stored as a contiguous 
block of [memory](computer_science/computer_memory) or as a chain of linked nodes. Any concrete realization 
that provides those operations with the agreed behavior is a valid implementation of that abstract data type.

nodes.title: bit_field
nodes.content:
# bit_field


[bit_field](computer_science/bit_field) is a [data structure](computer_science/data_structure) that consists of one or 
more adjacent [bits](computer_science/bit) which have been allocated for specific purposes, so that any 
single bit or group of bits within the structure can be set or inspected.

---

For example, a 3-bit field can store three independent permission flags - read, write, and 
execute - one per bit. Setting the read bit to 1 grants read access, clearing it to 0 revokes read access, 
and the same idea applies independently to the write and execute bits. Because each flag occupies its own bit, all 
three can be inspected or changed in a single operation without disturbing the others.

nodes.title: collection
nodes.content:
# collection


[collection](computer_science/collection) is an [abstract data type](computer_science/abstract_data_type) that groups a 
variable number of [items](mathematics/item) (possibly zero) that share some significance and need to be 
[operated](computer_science/operation) upon together in a controlled fashion.

---

A collection of three items supports adding a new item, removing one that is no longer needed, and asking how many 
items it currently holds. Different kinds of collections impose different rules - some keep the items in the order they 
were added, some prevent duplicates - but all of them treat the grouped items as a single unit that can be processed 
together.

nodes.title: map
nodes.content:
# map


[map](computer_science/map) is a [data structure](computer_science/data_structure) that associates each key 
[item](mathematics/item) with at most one value item. It models the mathematical 
[function](mathematics/function) abstraction, where the set of keys forms the function's domain and 
each key maps to exactly one value.

---

For example, a map from student names to exam scores might contain the pairs ("Alice", 92), ("Bob", 85), and 
("Carol", 78). Looking up the key "Alice" returns the value 92; looking up a key that is not present (such as "Dan") 
returns nothing. Assigning "Alice" a second time replaces 92 with the new value, which is what keeps the "at most one 
value per key" rule intact.

nodes.title: primitive_data_type
nodes.content:
# primitive_data_type


[primitive_data_type](computer_science/primitive_data_type) is a basic [data type](computer_science/data_type) whose values are atomic and 
cannot be decomposed into simpler parts. The [set](mathematics/set) of primitive data types forms the 
foundation from which all other data types are constructed.

---

For example, a primitive data type might represent truth values (with only two possible values), individual characters, 
or whole [numbers](mathematics/number) within a fixed range. Each value of such a type is treated as an indivisible unit: unlike a composite 
type, it cannot be broken down into smaller named components.

nodes.title: associative_array
nodes.content:
# associative_array


An [abstract data type](computer_science/abstract_data_type) that 
[maps](computer_science/map) keys to values. It is a [collection](computer_science/collection) 
of key-value pairs, where each key is [unique](mathematics/uniqueness) and is used to access the 
corresponding value. Associative arrays allow for efficient [operations](computer_science/operation): 
retrieval, insertion, and deletion of values based on their keys.

---

For example, a phone book can be modeled as an associative array where each person's name serves as the key and their 
phone number as the value. Looking up the key "Alice" retrieves her number, inserting a new contact adds a new 
key-value pair, and deleting "Alice" removes her entry. Because each key must be unique, assigning a second number 
to "Alice" replaces the previous value rather than creating a duplicate entry.

nodes.title: bag
nodes.content:
# bag


A bag is a [collection](computer_science/collection) that allows for the storage of multiple 
[items](mathematics/item), where the same item can be stored multiple times. It realizes the 
[multiset](mathematics/multiset) abstraction as an 
[abstract data type](computer_science/abstract_data_type), but focuses on the operations of adding items and 
[iterating](mathematics/iteration) over them; removing items is not supported.

---

For example, a bag collecting exam scores might hold (72, 85, 72, 90): the score 72 appears twice, and that 
multiplicity is preserved. A program can add more scores and walk through every stored item, but it cannot remove a 
specific one.

nodes.title: set
nodes.content:
# set


A set is an [abstract data type](computer_science/abstract_data_type) that can store 
[unique](mathematics/uniqueness) values, without any particular order. It is a computer 
implementation of the mathematical concept of a [finite set](mathematics/finite_set). Unlike most 
other [collection](computer_science/collection) types, rather than retrieving a specific element from a 
set, one typically tests a value for membership in a set.

---

For example, a set might store the registered usernames {"alice", "bob", "carol"}. Adding "alice" again has no 
effect, since a value can appear at most once. The main operation is testing whether a name belongs to the set: 
asking "is bob a member?" returns yes, while "is dan a member?" returns no.

nodes.title: list
nodes.content:
# list


An ordered [collection](computer_science/collection). Also known as a 
[sequence](mathematics/sequence). One can add, remove, and pop any element from the list. A list 
can store elements of different [types](computer_science/data_type).

---

For example, a list holding the exam scores [72, 85, 90] keeps them in that exact order. Adding 91 to the end 
produces [72, 85, 90, 91], removing 85 leaves [72, 90, 91], and popping the last element returns 91 and leaves 
[72, 90]. Because order matters, [72, 85, 90] is a different list from [90, 85, 72].

nodes.title: edge_case
nodes.content:
# edge case


An [edge_case](computer_science/edge_case) is a [test case](computer_science/test_case) designed to cover unusual or
[boundary](mathematics/bound) [conditions](mathematics/criterion) where a system, 
[algorithm](mathematics/algorithm), or [function](mathematics/function) 
may behave differently.

---

For a function that finds the smallest item in a [list](computer_science/list), the edge cases include the empty
list (no item to choose), a single-element list (only one candidate), and a list where every item is equal (no
unique smallest). Each sits at a boundary the function must handle without crashing or returning a wrong result.

nodes.title: special_case
nodes.content:
# special case


A [special_case](computer_science/special_case) is a particular [test case](computer_science/test_case) that satisfies additional
[conditions](mathematics/criterion), making it a more specific situation within a broader category.

Special cases may be related to [edge cases](computer_science/edge_case), but they are not necessarily 
[boundary](mathematics/bound) conditions.

---

Within the broad category "integer", the special case "even [integer](mathematics/integer)" adds
the condition "divisible by 2". A [function](mathematics/function) written for all integers may need separate handling 
for the even special case — for example, an integer is even exactly when its last 
[binary digit](computer_science/bit) is 0, so the check can be done with a single 
[bitwise](computer_science/bitwise_operation) test instead of division.

nodes.title: array
nodes.content:
# array


Array is a [list](computer_science/list) of elements of the same 
[type](computer_science/data_type), stored contiguously so that each element can be accessed directly by 
its [index](mathematics/index).

---

For example, an array holding the scores [72, 85, 90, 91] stores them in one contiguous block where the value at 
index 0 is 72, at index 1 is 85, and so on. Reading or replacing the value at a given index takes the same time no 
matter where it sits, because the index directly determines the element's position.

nodes.title: random_access_memory
nodes.content:
# random access memory


[random_access_memory](computer_science/random_access_memory) is a type of [computer_memory](computer_science/computer_memory) that allows [data](computer_science/data) 
to be read or written in almost the same amount of time regardless of the physical location of the data within the 
memory. This enables fast access to any memory location, making it suitable for storing data that needs to be 
quickly accessed and modified during [program](computer_science/program) execution.

---

When a [processor](computer_science/processor) reads element 5 of a million-element [array](computer_science/array), it reaches 
that location just as fast as element 0 — there is no need to scan through the preceding elements first. 
This constant-time access is what lets programs index into arrays and other 
[data structures](computer_science/data_structure) without slowdown.

nodes.title: hash_table
nodes.content:
# hash_table


[Data structure](computer_science/data_structure) that implements 
[associative array](computer_science/associative_array) using a 
[hash function](mathematics/hash_function) to compute an [index](mathematics/index) 
into an [array](computer_science/array) of buckets or slots, from which the desired value can be found.

---

For example, to store a phone book in a hash table, the key "Alice" is passed through a hash function that produces 
an index such as 42. The pair ("Alice", "555-0100") is then stored at position 42 in the underlying array. To retrieve 
Alice's number later, the same key is hashed again to obtain index 42, and the value is read directly from that 
position, making lookup very fast on average.

nodes.title: hash_set
nodes.content:
# hash_set


A hash set is a [set](computer_science/set) implementation that uses a 
[hash table](computer_science/hash_table) to store [unique](mathematics/uniqueness) 
elements. It maps each element through a hash-based structure so membership tests, insertions, and removals can 
usually be performed [efficiently](mathematics/efficiency).

---

For example, a hash set of registered usernames {"alice", "bob", "carol"} stores only the names themselves, with 
no associated values. To check whether "bob" is already registered, the name is hashed to locate a position in the 
underlying [array](computer_science/array), and the stored element at that position is compared directly. 
Adding "alice" a second time is detected and ignored, keeping each name present at most once.

nodes.title: subarray
nodes.content:
# subarray


A contiguous [subsequence](mathematics/subsequence) of an 
[array](computer_science/array) A of length n. A subarray is determined by two 
[indices](mathematics/index) l and r with 0 <= l <= r < n, and contains exactly the 
elements A[l], A[l+1], ..., A[r] in their original order.

---

For example, [2, 3, 4] is a subarray of [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], while [1, 3, 5] is not because its elements are not 
adjacent in the original array.

nodes.title: linked_list
nodes.content:
# linked_list


A [list](computer_science/list) implemented as an ordered [collection](computer_science/collection) 
of elements. Each element is stored in a [node](mathematics/node) that contains a 
[reference](computer_science/pointer) to the next node. Linked lists can be singly linked or doubly linked, 
depending on whether each node has a reference to the next node only or both the next and previous nodes.

---

For example, a singly linked list holding the values 7, 9, and 2 consists of three nodes: the first stores 7 and a 
link to the second, the second stores 9 and a link to the third, and the third stores 2 with a link pointing to 
nothing (the end of the list). Starting from the first node and following each link visits the values in order. 
In a doubly linked list, each node would also carry a backward link to the previous node.

nodes.title: lru_cache
nodes.content:
# LRU cache


An LRU cache is a [cache](computer_science/cache) that keeps recently used entries and removes the 
least recently used entry when it needs space for a new one. A common implementation combines a 
[hash table](computer_science/hash_table) for fast lookup with a 
[linked list](computer_science/linked_list) that records entries from most recently used to least 
recently used. Read and write [operations](computer_science/operation) update that recency order.

---

For example, an LRU cache with capacity 3 receives the accesses A, B, C, A, D in that order. After A, B, C the cache 
holds {A, B, C} with C most recent. Accessing A again moves it to most recent, giving {B, C, A}. Adding D now needs 
space, so the least recently used entry B is evicted and the cache becomes {C, A, D}.

nodes.title: circular_linked_list
nodes.content:
# circular linked list


A [circular_linked_list](computer_science/circular_linked_list) is a [linked list](computer_science/linked_list) in which the last 
[node](mathematics/node) points back to the first node.

This forms a [cycle](mathematics/cycle) and allows traversal to wrap around indefinitely.

---

For example, three nodes holding 7, 9, and 2 can be linked so that the last node points back to the first: 
7 → 9 → 2 → (back to 7). Starting at the node holding 7 and following each link visits 7, 9, 2, 7, 9, 2, ... 
repeating forever instead of reaching an end.

nodes.title: queue
nodes.content:
# queue


Queue is a [data structure](computer_science/data_structure) providing 
[first_in_first_out](mathematics/first_in_first_out) semantics. Serves as a [collection](computer_science/collection) 
of elements with two main [operations](computer_science/operation):
- Enqueue, which adds an element to the rear of the queue, and
- Dequeue, which removes an element from the front.
Additionally, a peek [operation](computer_science/operation) can, without modifying the queue, return 
the value of the next element to be dequeued without dequeuing it.

---

Starting empty, enqueueing A, then B, then C places them in the queue in that order. The first dequeue removes A, 
the element added earliest; the next removes B; the last removes C. The element that has waited longest is always the 
one removed next.

nodes.title: conceptual_test
nodes.content:
# conceptual test


A [conceptual_test](computer_science/conceptual_test) is a [test](computer_science/test) used to check understanding of an idea,
model, or design, rather than to execute [code](computer_science/code).

A conceptual test evaluates whether some [criteria](mathematics/criterion) are satisfied.

---

Before writing any code, a designer might ask: "If the [queue](computer_science/queue) is empty and we try to remove
an element, what should happen?" Answering "it should report that there is nothing to remove, not crash" is a
conceptual test — it checks that the design handles the empty case correctly, without yet building anything.

nodes.title: priority_queue
nodes.content:
# priority_queue


A priority queue is an [abstract data type](computer_science/abstract_data_type) that operates similarly 
to a regular [queue](computer_science/queue) but with an added feature: each element in the priority 
queue has a 'priority' associated with it. Elements with higher priority are served before elements with lower 
priority. If two elements have the same priority, they are served according to their 
[first_in_first_out](mathematics/first_in_first_out) order.

---

Suppose four tasks arrive in order A (priority 1), B (priority 3), C (priority 3), D (priority 2), where a higher 
[number](mathematics/number) means higher priority. They are served in the order B, C, D, A: B and C 
share the highest priority, so they are served in the order they arrived; then D; finally A, the lowest priority, 
is served last.

nodes.title: stack
nodes.content:
# stack


Stack is a [data structure](computer_science/data_structure) providing 
[last_in_first_out](mathematics/last_in_first_out) semantics; also called a LIFO 
[queue](computer_science/queue). Serves as a [collection](computer_science/collection) 
of elements with two main [operations](computer_science/operation):
- Push, which adds an element to the collection, and
- Pop, which removes the most recently added element.
Additionally, a peek [operation](computer_science/operation) can, without modifying the stack, return 
the value of the last element added. The name stack is an analogy to a [set](mathematics/set) of 
physical items stacked one atop another, such as a stack of plates.

---

Starting empty, pushing A, then B, then C places C on top. The first pop removes C, the most recently added element; 
the next removes B; the last removes A. The element added last is always the one removed next.

nodes.title: boolean
nodes.content:
# boolean


Boolean (sometimes shortened to Bool) is a [primitive data type](computer_science/primitive_data_type) 
that has one of two possible values usually denoted true and false. Boolean is a 
[bit field](computer_science/bit_field) that stores a single [bit](computer_science/bit) of 
[information](mathematics/information).

---

A boolean can represent whether a light is on (true) or off (false). Since there are only two possibilities, a 
single bit suffices to distinguish them.

nodes.title: character
nodes.content:
# character


A [character](computer_science/character) is a [primitive data type](computer_science/primitive_data_type) that represents 
a single textual symbol, such as a letter, digit, or punctuation mark. It is the atomic unit of 
[information](mathematics/information) from which text is composed.

---

The symbols `A`, `7`, and `?` are each a single character. A piece of text such as `Hello` is built from five 
characters taken together, and each one can be inspected, compared, or replaced independently of the others.

nodes.title: integer
nodes.content:
# integer


A [primitive data type](computer_science/primitive_data_type) that represents whole 
[numbers](mathematics/number), i.e. [integers](mathematics/integer) stored in a 
fixed amount of memory. Integers can be positive, negative, or zero.

---

A signed 8-[bit](computer_science/bit) integer can store values from -128 to 127. The value 42 fits, while 200 does not, because it exceeds 
the range that 8 bits can hold.

nodes.title: character_encoding
nodes.content:
# character_encoding


A method of representing [characters](computer_science/character) as numerical values, allowing computers to 
store and manipulate text. Character encoding schemes define the [mapping](computer_science/map) between 
characters and their corresponding [numerical](mathematics/number) values.

---

Under one encoding, the [character](computer_science/character) `A` is assigned the number 65, `B` is 
assigned 66, and so on. Storing the text `AB` then means storing the two numbers 65 and 66, which can later be mapped 
back to the original characters.

nodes.title: ascii
nodes.content:
# ascii


ASCII is a [character encoding](computer_science/character_encoding) standard that uses 7 
[bits](computer_science/bit) to represent 128 [characters](computer_science/character), 
including letters, digits, punctuation marks, and control characters.

---

In ASCII, the uppercase letter `A` is assigned the value 65, `B` is 66, the digit `0` is 48, and the space character 
is 32. Since only 7 bits are used, the highest assignable value is 127.

nodes.title: extended_ascii
nodes.content:
# extended_ascii


An extension of the [ASCII](computer_science/ascii) 
[character encoding](computer_science/character_encoding) standard that uses 8 
[bits](computer_science/bit) to represent 256 [characters](computer_science/character), including 
additional symbols and characters from various languages.

---

The first 128 code points match ASCII exactly, so the value 65 still represents `A`. The remaining 128 code points 
(values 128-255) are used for additional symbols, such as accented letters and box-drawing characters.

nodes.title: unicode
nodes.content:
# unicode


A [character encoding](computer_science/character_encoding) standard that aims to provide a 
[unique](mathematics/uniqueness) [number](mathematics/number) for every 
[character](computer_science/character), regardless of the system.

---

Each character is assigned a code point, written as U+ followed by a hexadecimal number. For example, `A` is 
assigned U+0041, the digit `0` is U+0030, and the symbol `€` is U+20AC. No two characters share the same code point.

nodes.title: utf
nodes.content:
# utf


UTF (Unicode Transformation Format) is a [character encoding](computer_science/character_encoding) 
standard that represents [Unicode](computer_science/unicode) 
[characters](computer_science/character) using variable-length 
[sequences](mathematics/sequence) of bytes.

---

The character `A` (code point U+0041) is represented by a single byte, while `€` (code point U+20AC) requires three 
bytes. Characters with higher code points may need up to four bytes, so the [number](mathematics/number) 
of bytes per character varies.

nodes.title: utf_8
nodes.content:
# utf_8


A [UTF](computer_science/utf) [character encoding](computer_science/character_encoding) 
scheme that uses 8-[bit](computer_science/bit) code units, meaning each unit is one byte. A 
[Unicode](computer_science/unicode) [character](computer_science/character) is encoded as 1 to 4 
such units. It is backward compatible with [ASCII](computer_science/ascii) and can represent any character 
in the Unicode standard.

---

The character `A` (code point U+0041) is encoded as a single 8-bit unit, matching its ASCII representation. The 
character `€` (code point U+20AC) is encoded as three units, while rarer characters may need up to four units.

nodes.title: string
nodes.content:
# string


A [sequence](mathematics/sequence) of [characters](computer_science/character), typically 
used to represent text. Strings can be of variable length and can contain letters, 
[numbers](mathematics/number), symbols, and whitespace.

---

The text `Hello` is a string made up of the characters `H`, `e`, `l`, `l`, `o` in that order. To store it, a 
[character encoding](computer_science/character_encoding) assigns each character a numerical value; for 
example, `H` may map to 72 and `e` to 101, so the string is recorded as the corresponding sequence of numbers and 
can later be decoded back into the original text.

nodes.title: isomorphic_string
nodes.content:
# isomorphic string


Two [strings](computer_science/string) are isomorphic when the 
[characters](computer_science/character) of one string can be replaced to obtain the other string using a 
consistent one-to-one mapping. This mapping is an [isomorphism](mathematics/isomorphism) between the 
character patterns of the strings: each character in the first string maps to exactly one character in the second 
string, and no two different characters map to the same character.

---

The strings `egg` and `add` are isomorphic: `e` maps to `a` and `g` maps to `d`, so replacing each character in `egg` 
by its partner yields `add`. The strings `foo` and `bar` are not isomorphic: `f` maps to `b` and `o` maps to `a`, but 
the second `o` would need to map to `r`, contradicting the one-to-one rule since `o` already maps to `a`.

nodes.title: anagram
nodes.content:
# anagram


An anagram is a [string](computer_science/string) formed by 
[rearranging](mathematics/reordering) the [characters](computer_science/character) of another 
string. Equivalently, two strings are anagrams when one is a [permutation](mathematics/permutation) of 
the other and both strings have the same [multiset](mathematics/multiset) of characters.

---

The strings `listen` and `silent` are anagrams: both contain exactly the same characters (one `s`, one `i`, one `l`, 
one `e`, one `n`, one `t`), and `silent` is a reordering of `listen`. The strings `hello` and `world` are not 
anagrams, since they contain different characters and therefore different multisets.

nodes.title: levenshtein_distance
nodes.content:
# Levenshtein distance


Levenshtein distance is the minimum [number](mathematics/number) of 
single-[character](computer_science/character) [operations](computer_science/operation) 
needed to transform one [string](computer_science/string) into another, where each operation is an 
insertion, deletion, or substitution.

---

The Levenshtein distance between `kitten` and `sitting` is 3: substitute `k` with `s`, substitute `e` with `i`, and 
insert `g` at the end. The distance between `flaw` and `lawn` is 2: delete `f`, and insert `n` at the end.

nodes.title: string_concatenation
nodes.content:
# string concatenation


[String concatenation](computer_science/string_concatenation) is the [operation](mathematics/operation) of 
joining two or more [strings](computer_science/string) end-to-end to form a new string.

---

Concatenating `foo` and `bar` yields `foobar`. Concatenating `hello`, a single space ` `, and `world` yields 
`hello world`.

nodes.title: head_insertion
nodes.content:
# head insertion


[Head insertion](computer_science/head_insertion), also called prepending, is an 
[operation](mathematics/operation) that adds an [item](mathematics/item) to the 
beginning of a [list](computer_science/list). In a [linked list](computer_science/linked_list), 
head insertion commonly creates a new [node](mathematics/node), points it to the previous first node, 
and updates the head [pointer](computer_science/pointer) to the new node.

---

Given a linked list `B -> C` with head pointing to `B`, head insertion of `A` creates a new node `A`, points it to 
`B`, and moves the head pointer to `A`, yielding `A -> B -> C`. The item is now first, and the rest of the list 
follows unchanged.

nodes.title: substring
nodes.content:
# substring


A contiguous [subsequence](mathematics/subsequence) of 
[characters](computer_science/character) within a [string](computer_science/string). Unlike a 
subsequence, the selected characters must appear next to each other in the original string.

---

In the string `It was the best of times`, the segment `the best of` is a substring because its characters appear 
consecutively. By contrast, `I was times` is not a substring, since those words are not adjacent, even though they 
appear in order.

nodes.title: regular_expression
nodes.content:
# regular expression


A [regular_expression](computer_science/regular_expression) is a [sequence](mathematics/sequence) of 
[characters](computer_science/character) that defines a search pattern for 
[strings](computer_science/string). Regular expressions use special syntax — including literal characters, 
character classes (sets like `[0-9]`), quantifiers (such as `+` or `*`), and anchors (such as `^` and `$`) — 
to specify patterns for matching, searching, and manipulating text. 
Groups and [labels](mathematics/label) can capture and reference parts of the matched text.

---

The pattern `[0-9]+` matches one or more digits, so it finds [substrings](computer_science/substring) such 
as `42` or `7` inside a longer string. The pattern `^[a-z]+$` matches only strings that consist entirely of lowercase 
letters from start to end, such as `hello` but not `Hello123`.

nodes.title: trie
nodes.content:
# trie


A type of [tree](mathematics/tree) data structure used to store a dynamic 
[set](mathematics/set) of [strings](computer_science/string), where each 
[node](mathematics/node) represents a single [character](computer_science/character) of a 
string. The path from the [root](mathematics/root) to a node represents a prefix shared by every 
string that passes through it. The main advantage of a trie is efficient retrieval of strings with common prefixes.

---

Storing the words `tea`, `ten`, and `in` starts at a root node. Under the root, a child `t` and a child `i` branch 
off. From `t`, a child `e` is added, which then has two children `a` and `n` to complete `tea` and `ten`. From `i`, a 
child `n` completes `in`. Looking up any word means walking from the root along its characters one node at a time.

nodes.title: graph_labeling
nodes.content:
# graph_labeling


A [problem](mathematics/problem) of assigning [labels](mathematics/label), traditionally 
represented by [integers](computer_science/integer), to [edges](mathematics/edge) and/or 
[nodes](mathematics/node) of a [graph](mathematics/graph).

---

In a [graph](mathematics/graph) with three [nodes](mathematics/node) connected in a 
triangle, one labeling assigns the integer 1 to the first node, 2 to the second, and 3 to the third, while another 
assigns 0, 0, and 1. Each assignment is a valid labeling; whether it satisfies a given rule depends on the specific 
problem, such as requiring adjacent nodes to receive different labels.

nodes.title: graph_coloring
nodes.content:
# graph_coloring


A special case of [graph labeling](computer_science/graph_labeling) where the 
[labels](mathematics/label) are colors. The specific rule that the colors must satisfy — such as 
requiring connected elements to differ — defines the particular variant of the 
[problem](mathematics/problem).

---

Assigning the colors red, green, and blue to the three [nodes](mathematics/node) of a triangle gives 
a coloring. Whether it is a valid [solution](mathematics/solution) depends on the rule: one variant may 
require that any two nodes joined by an [edge](mathematics/edge) receive different colors, while another 
may impose no such [constraint](mathematics/constraint).

nodes.title: vertex_coloring
nodes.content:
# vertex_coloring


A specific type of [graph coloring](computer_science/graph_coloring) where the goal is to ensure that 
no two [nodes](mathematics/node) joined by an [edge](mathematics/edge) share the same 
color.

---

In a triangle with [nodes](mathematics/node) A, B, and C, each pair is joined by an 
[edge](mathematics/edge), so all three need different colors: A red, B green, C blue. In a path 
A-B-C, only A-B and B-C are joined by edges, so A and C can share a color: A red, B green, C red.

nodes.title: hash_collision
nodes.content:
# hash_collision


A situation in which two different [inputs](mathematics/input_data) produce the same 
[hash value](mathematics/hash) when processed by a 
[hash function](mathematics/hash_function). This can lead to 
[data](computer_science/data) integrity issues and is a key consideration in the design of hash functions 
and [hash tables](computer_science/hash_table).

---

Under a [hash function](mathematics/hash_function) that returns the last digit of a 
[number](mathematics/number), the [inputs](mathematics/input_data) 17 and 27 both 
produce the [hash](mathematics/hash) 7, so they collide. When stored in a 
[hash table](computer_science/hash_table), both entries land in the same slot, which the table must resolve 
(for example by chaining) so that neither value is lost.

nodes.title: rolling_hash
nodes.content:
# rolling_hash


A rolling hash is an approach designed to enable efficient execution of the 
[hash function](mathematics/hash_function) when the input is modified incrementally, such as when 
a window of fixed size moves over a [sequence](mathematics/sequence).

---

A naive [hash function](mathematics/hash_function) recomputes the hash of each length-3 window in 
the [sequence](mathematics/sequence) `[4, 7, 2, 9, 1]` from scratch, hashing `[4, 7, 2]`, then 
`[7, 2, 9]`, then `[2, 9, 1]` independently. A rolling hash instead updates the previous hash when the window slides: 
removing the contribution of `4`, shifting, and adding the contribution of `9` turns the hash of `[4, 7, 2]` into the 
hash of `[7, 2, 9]` in constant time, without reprocessing the overlapping `7` and `2`.

nodes.title: rabin_karp_algorithm
nodes.content:
# rabin_karp_algorithm


A string searching [algorithm](mathematics/algorithm) that uses a 
[rolling hash](computer_science/rolling_hash) to find a pattern in a 
[string](computer_science/string). It computes the [hash](mathematics/hash_function) of the 
pattern and the hash of each [substring](computer_science/substring) of the text of the same length as the 
pattern, and compares them to find matches. Because two different substrings may share the same hash, the algorithm 
checks the [characters](computer_science/character) directly whenever a hash match occurs to confirm a real 
match and avoid false positives from [hash collisions](computer_science/hash_collision).

---

To search for the pattern `abc` in the text `zabcab`, the algorithm hashes `abc`, then hashes each length-3 
[substring](computer_science/substring) of the text (`zab`, `abc`, `bca`, `cab`) using a 
[rolling hash](computer_science/rolling_hash) so that each new window's hash is computed from the previous 
one. Only when a window's hash equals the pattern's hash does the algorithm compare the characters to confirm the 
match.

nodes.title: bit_manipulation
nodes.content:
# bit manipulation


[bit_manipulation](computer_science/bit_manipulation) is a technique that uses [bitwise operations](computer_science/bitwise_operation) 
to perform direct operations on individual [bits](computer_science/bit) or groups of bits in a 
[binary representation](computer_science/binary_representation). It is commonly used in 
[algorithms](mathematics/algorithm) for tasks like setting, clearing, toggling, or checking specific 
bits, as well as performing [efficient](mathematics/efficiency) computations.

---

To check whether the third bit of `1010` is set, a mask `0100` is applied with a bitwise AND: `1010 AND 0100` yields 
`0000`, so the bit is 0. To set that same bit, a mask `0100` is applied with a bitwise OR: `1010 OR 0100` yields 
`1110`, turning the bit on without changing the others.

nodes.title: kadanes_algorithm
nodes.content:
# Kadane's algorithm


Kadane's algorithm is an [algorithm](mathematics/algorithm) for finding a contiguous 
[subarray](computer_science/subarray) with maximum sum in a [numeric](mathematics/number) 
[sequence](mathematics/sequence). It uses a 
[dynamic programming](mathematics/dynamic_programming) recurrence that tracks the best subarray ending 
at the current position and the best subarray seen so far, producing an 
[optimized](mathematics/optimization) linear-time solution to the maximum subarray problem.

---

For the [sequence](mathematics/sequence) `[-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]`, Kadane's algorithm walks 
left to right, at each step choosing between extending the current subarray or starting fresh. At each position it 
keeps the best sum ending there (`current`) and the best sum seen so far (`best`):

  -2:  current = max(-2, 0 + -2) = -2,  best = -2   (start fresh)
   1:  current = max( 1, -2 +  1) =  1,  best =  1   (start fresh)
  -3:  current = max(-3,  1 + -3) = -2,  best =  1   (extend; best unchanged)
   4:  current = max( 4, -2 +  4) =  4,  best =  4   (start fresh)
  -1:  current = max(-1,  4 + -1) =  3,  best =  4   (extend)
   2:  current = max( 2,  3 +  2) =  5,  best =  5   (extend)
   1:  current = max( 1,  5 +  1) =  6,  best =  6   (extend)
  -5:  current = max(-5,  6 + -5) =  1,  best =  6   (extend; best unchanged)
   4:  current = max( 4,  1 +  4) =  5,  best =  6   (extend; best unchanged)

The best [subarray](computer_science/subarray) ends where `best` reached 6, at the element `1`, tracing 
back to `[4, -1, 2, 1]` — whose sum is 6, larger than any other contiguous subarray in the sequence.

nodes.title: mantissa
nodes.content:
# mantissa


[Mantissa](computer_science/mantissa) (also called significand) is the part of a floating-point 
[number](mathematics/number) that holds its significant digits, determining the precision of the 
value. Together with a sign and an exponent, the mantissa encodes the full number: the exponent sets the scale 
(magnitude) while the mantissa sets the significant digits that are kept.

---

In the scientific notation value 6.022 x 10^23, the mantissa is 6.022 and the exponent is 23. Because a fixed 
[number of bits](computer_science/bit) is allocated to the mantissa, only a limited count of significant 
digits can be stored; any digits beyond that are rounded away.

nodes.title: float
nodes.content:
# Float


[Float](computer_science/float) is a floating-point [data type](computer_science/data_type) used 
to represent an approximation of a [real number](mathematics/real_number) with finite precision.

---

A float can hold common values such as 3.14 (an approximation of pi) and 2.5, as well as very large
magnitudes such as 6.022e23 and very small ones such as 1.6e-19, since it uses a sign bit, an exponent, and a
[mantissa](computer_science/mantissa) to encode the value.

nodes.title: floating_point_precision
nodes.content:
# floating-point precision


[Floating-point precision](computer_science/floating_point_precision) is the limited accuracy with which a 
[float](computer_science/float) can represent a 
[real number](mathematics/real_number), which causes rounding errors in computations.

Many decimal fractions have no exact finite representation as 
[binary fractions](computer_science/binary_fractions). For example, the decimal value 0.1 is a repeating
fraction in binary (0.0001100110011...), so it cannot be stored exactly and is instead held as the nearest
representable approximation.

---

Because 0.1 is stored approximately, adding it to itself three times does not produce exactly 0.3:
0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.30000000000000004. In contrast, values such as 0.5 and 0.25 are stored exactly, because they
are negative powers of two (2^-1 and 2^-2).

nodes.title: double
nodes.content:
# Double


[Double](computer_science/double) (short for double precision) is a floating-point
[data type](computer_science/data_type) used to represent an approximation of a
[real number](mathematics/real_number) with finite precision. In many systems, a double provides
about twice the precision of a [float](computer_science/float) because it allocates more
[bits](computer_science/bit) to its [mantissa](computer_science/mantissa) and exponent.

---

A 32-bit single-precision float typically keeps about 7 significant decimal digits, while a 64-bit double keeps
about 15-16. For example, the constant pi (approximately 3.14159265358979) can be stored more accurately in a
double than in a float, because its larger mantissa retains more significant bits.

nodes.title: auxiliary_space
nodes.content:
# auxiliary space


[auxiliary_space](computer_science/auxiliary_space) is the extra [memory](computer_science/computer_memory) an
[algorithm](mathematics/algorithm) uses beyond the space needed to store its 
[input](mathematics/input_data) (or output).

---

An algorithm that processes its input using only a fixed number of temporary values has constant auxiliary space,
regardless of how large the input grows. In contrast, an algorithm that builds a full copy of its input into a
separate structure uses auxiliary memory that grows in proportion to the input size.

nodes.title: in_place_algorithm
