nodes.content:
# in-place algorithm


An [algorithm](mathematics/algorithm) that transforms a 
[data structure](computer_science/data_structure) using only a constant amount of 
[auxiliary space](computer_science/auxiliary_space), meaning it 
[operates](computer_science/operation) directly on the [input data](mathematics/input_data) 
rather than creating a separate copy. An in-place algorithm typically has a 
[space complexity](mathematics/space_complexity) of [O(1)](mathematics/big_o_notation), 
not counting the space used by the input itself.

---

Reversing an [array](computer_science/array) in place is done by swapping the first and last elements, then
the second and second-to-last, and so on, moving toward the middle. The array is modified directly, using only a
single temporary variable to hold one value during each swap, so the auxiliary space stays constant regardless of
the array's length.

nodes.title: xor_swap_algorithm
nodes.content:
# XOR swap algorithm


The XOR swap algorithm is an [algorithm](mathematics/algorithm) that swaps the values of two 
[variables](computer_science/variable) by applying three [XOR](mathematics/xor) 
[bitwise operations](computer_science/bitwise_operation). It is a 
[bit manipulation](computer_science/bit_manipulation) technique and an 
[in-place algorithm](computer_science/in_place_algorithm) because it exchanges the values without using 
an additional temporary variable.

---

Swapping two values a = 5 (0101) and b = 3 (0011) takes three XOR steps. First, a = a XOR b becomes 0110. Second,
b = a XOR b becomes 0101, which is the original value of a. Third, a = a XOR b becomes 0011, which is the original
value of b. The values are now exchanged using only XOR, with no temporary variable.

nodes.title: boyer_moore_majority_vote_algorithm
nodes.content:
# Boyer-Moore majority vote algorithm


An [algorithm](mathematics/algorithm) that finds the 
[majority element](mathematics/majority_element) in a [sequence](mathematics/sequence) 
using a single pass through the data. It is an [in-place algorithm](computer_science/in_place_algorithm) 
that maintains two [variables](computer_science/variable): a candidate element and a counter. The algorithm 
[iterates](mathematics/loop) through the sequence; when the counter is zero it sets the current 
element as the candidate, then increments the counter if the current element matches the candidate or decrements it 
otherwise. It has a [time complexity](mathematics/time_complexity) of 
[O(n)](mathematics/big_o_notation) and a [space complexity](mathematics/space_complexity) 
of [O(1)](mathematics/big_o_notation).

---

For the sequence (1, 1, 2, 2, 2), the algorithm starts with candidate unset and counter 0. Reading left to
right:
- element 1: candidate = 1, counter = 1
- element 1: candidate = 1, counter = 2
- element 2: candidate = 1, counter = 1
- element 2: candidate = 1, counter = 0
- element 2: candidate = 2, counter = 1
With counter above zero the surviving candidate is 2, which is the majority element.

nodes.title: two_pointers_technique
nodes.content:
# two pointers technique


A problem-solving [algorithmic](mathematics/algorithm) approach used on a 
[sequence](mathematics/sequence) (typically an [array](computer_science/array)) 
that maintains two [pointers](computer_science/pointer) (or 
[indices](mathematics/index)) which traverse the data simultaneously. The pointers 
commonly start at opposite ends and move toward each other, or move in the same direction at 
different speeds (a "fast" and "slow" pointer). Each iteration of the 
[loop](mathematics/loop) advances one or both pointers based on a condition until they 
meet or the target configuration is found. It is an 
[in-place algorithm](computer_science/in_place_algorithm) that typically reduces a problem 
requiring nested iteration from a [time complexity](mathematics/time_complexity) of 
[O(n^2)](mathematics/big_o_notation) to [O(n)](mathematics/big_o_notation) 
while maintaining a [space complexity](mathematics/space_complexity) of 
[O(1)](mathematics/big_o_notation).

---

To find two values in a [sorted](mathematics/sorting) [array](computer_science/array) that
sum to a target, one pointer starts at the left end and another at the right end. Their values are added together:
if the sum is too small, the left pointer advances rightward to a larger value; if too large, the right pointer
moves leftward to a smaller value. On the array [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8] searching for a sum of 10, the pointers skip
past the 1, then settle on 2 and 8, the pair whose sum equals the target.

nodes.title: floyds_tortoise_and_hare_algorithm
nodes.content:
# Floyd's Tortoise and Hare algorithm


Floyd's Tortoise and Hare algorithm is a [cycle detection](mathematics/cycle_detection) 
[algorithm](mathematics/algorithm) that uses the 
[two pointers technique](computer_science/two_pointers_technique). One 
[pointer](computer_science/pointer), the tortoise, advances one step at a time, while the other pointer, 
the hare, advances two steps at a time. If the two pointers meet, a [cycle](mathematics/cycle) exists; 
if the hare reaches the end, no cycle exists. It is commonly used to detect cycles in a 
[linked list](computer_science/linked_list).

---

Consider a [linked list](computer_science/linked_list) whose [nodes](mathematics/node) run
A then B then C then D, where D points back to B, forming a cycle. Both pointers start at A:
- After one step: tortoise at B, hare at C
- After two steps: tortoise at C, hare at B (having wrapped around)
- After three steps: tortoise at D, hare at D
Because the faster hare has caught the tortoise, a cycle is confirmed.

nodes.title: sliding_window_technique
nodes.content:
# sliding window technique


The sliding window technique is an [algorithmic](mathematics/algorithm) pattern for 
processing a [sequence](mathematics/sequence) by maintaining a contiguous window, often a 
[subarray](computer_science/subarray) or [substring](computer_science/substring), and moving 
its boundaries as the computation proceeds. It is commonly implemented as a specialized 
[two pointers technique](computer_science/two_pointers_technique): one boundary expands the window 
to include new elements, while the other boundary contracts it when the current window no longer satisfies a 
required condition.

---

To find the largest sum of any length-3 [subarray](computer_science/subarray) in the
[array](computer_science/array) [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], a window of size 3 slides one position at a time:
- window [2, 1, 5]: sum = 8
- window [1, 5, 1]: sum = 7
- window [5, 1, 3]: sum = 9
- window [1, 3, 2]: sum = 6
The maximum sum is 9, from the subarray [5, 1, 3]. At each step the window drops its leftmost value and adds the
next value on the right, so each sum is updated from the previous one instead of recomputed.

nodes.title: clustering
nodes.content:
# clustering


[clustering](computer_science/clustering) is the task of [partitioning](mathematics/partitioning) a 
[dataset](computer_science/dataset) into multiple groups (clusters) such that 
[items](mathematics/item) in the same cluster are more similar to each other than to items in other 
clusters.

The resulting clusters can be assigned a [label](mathematics/label) 
(e.g., a cluster id) for downstream use.

Clustering [algorithms](mathematics/algorithm) typically learn structure from unlabeled 
[data](computer_science/data).

---

Given a [dataset](computer_science/dataset) of customers each described by their monthly spending, a
clustering algorithm might form three groups: low spenders, medium spenders, and high spenders. Customers within a
single group have similar spending amounts, while customers in different groups differ noticeably. Each group can
then be assigned a [label](mathematics/label) such as "low", "medium", or "high" for later use.

nodes.title: lopsided
nodes.content:
# lopsided


[lopsided](computer_science/lopsided) describes a situation where something is unbalanced or heavily skewed toward one side.

In computer science, it often refers to a [data structure](computer_science/data_structure) or workload
whose shape or [distribution](mathematics/distribution) is highly uneven.

---

An [unbalanced binary tree](mathematics/unbalanced_binary_tree) is a lopsided data structure: one
side may contain a long chain of nodes while the other side is nearly empty, so the tree leans heavily toward one
side rather than spreading its nodes evenly.

nodes.title: null
nodes.content:
# null


[null](computer_science/null) is a special value that represents "no value" or 
"no [object](computer_science/object)".

It is often used to indicate that a [pointer](computer_science/pointer) does not refer to
a valid [memory](computer_science/computer_memory) location (i.e., it points to nothing).

---

In a [linked list](computer_science/linked_list), each [node](mathematics/node) holds a
[pointer](computer_science/pointer) to the next node. The last node has no successor, so its pointer is
set to null to mark the end of the list. Code that walks the list checks for null to know when to stop.

nodes.title: machine
nodes.content:
# machine


In computing, a [machine](computer_science/machine) is a physical or virtual [computer](computer_science/computer)
that can run [programs](computer_science/program) and perform 
[computation](mathematics/computation).

---

A laptop is a physical machine: its [hardware](computer_science/hardware) components, including a
[processor](computer_science/processor) that executes instructions, work together to run programs. A
virtual machine is also a machine, but it is implemented in software that emulates physical hardware, so programs
run on it as if it were real hardware.

nodes.title: operating_system
nodes.content:
# operating system


An [operating_system](computer_science/operating_system) is system software that manages a [computer](computer_science/computer)'s
[hardware](computer_science/hardware) and [software](computer_science/program) resources. It
allocates [memory](computer_science/computer_memory) to running programs, schedules their use of the
hardware, and provides services they rely on, such as [file storage](computer_science/file_storage)
and [input/output](computer_science/input_output).

---

When several programs run at once on a laptop, the operating system decides which one may use the processor next,
how much memory each receives, and how they take turns reading from the [disk](computer_science/disk). A program never touches the hardware
directly; instead it asks the operating system, which mediates access so the programs do not interfere with each
other.

nodes.title: process
nodes.content:
# process


A [process](computer_science/process) is an instance of a [program](computer_science/program)
that is being executed by the [operating system](computer_science/operating_system). When launched, a
process receives its own region of [memory](computer_science/computer_memory) for its code and data.

---

A [program](computer_science/program) is static code stored on disk, while a
[process](computer_science/process) is that program in motion. Running the same program twice creates two
processes, each with its own [memory](computer_science/computer_memory) and state, even though both came
from the same program.

nodes.title: thread
nodes.content:
# thread


A [thread](computer_science/thread) is a unit of execution within a [process](computer_science/process).

Threads within the same process typically share [memory](computer_science/computer_memory) and resources,
but can run different [operations](computer_science/operation).

---

A [process](computer_science/process) that handles a long computation while still accepting user input
can split the work across two [threads](computer_science/thread): one performs the computation, the other
listens for input. Because they belong to the same process they share 
[memory](computer_science/computer_memory), and because they run as separate threads the program achieves 
[concurrency](computer_science/concurrency) without starting a second process.

nodes.title: worker
nodes.content:
# worker


A [worker](computer_science/worker) is a [process](computer_science/process), 
[thread](computer_science/thread), or [machine](computer_science/machine) 
that performs a unit of work as part of a larger computation.

In distributed or [parallel](computer_science/parallelism) systems, workers execute parts of a
[program](computer_science/program) (tasks) assigned by a coordinator.

---

When a [program](computer_science/program) must process one thousand images, the work can be split across
four [threads](computer_science/thread), each acting as a worker that handles two hundred fifty images.
The workers run at the same time, so the [parallelism](computer_science/parallelism) lets the whole batch
finish roughly four times faster than a single worker would.

nodes.title: mapreduce
nodes.content:
# MapReduce


[mapreduce](computer_science/mapreduce) is a programming model for processing large [datasets](computer_science/dataset)
by splitting work into two phases:

- map: transform input records into intermediate key/value pairs (conceptually a [map](computer_science/map)).
- reduce: aggregate the intermediate values for each key.

MapReduce enables [parallelism](computer_science/parallelism) by distributing the map and reduce work across many
[workers](computer_science/worker).

---

To count how often each word appears in a large [dataset](computer_science/dataset) of documents, the map
phase turns each word it reads into a (word, 1) pair. The reduce phase then collects all pairs sharing a word and
adds their counts, producing a single (word, total) result per word. Because each 
[worker](computer_science/worker) handles a different slice of the documents, the counting is done in 
[parallel](computer_science/parallelism) and finishes much faster than reading the documents one by one.
